content:
The Sydney light rail was meant to cost 1.6 billion dollars and take four years. It will cost over 3 billion and take considerably longer. Businesses along the route have closed. Traffic patterns have been upended for years. The project has become, in the Australian tradition, a political football with blame distributed by tribal affiliation rather than competence.

I mention it because it's typical rather than unusual. Berlin's Brandenburg Airport was meant to open in 2011 and opened in 2020, at roughly three times budget. California's high-speed rail was costed at 33 billion dollars in 2008; the estimate now exceeds 100 billion and the line may never be finished. The pattern is global, it's consistent, and it's getting worse.

Something has happened to our ability to build things, and I think the something is more interesting than bad management or corruption, both of which are present and neither of which explains a factor of three. What we're watching is a civilisational process with historical precedent, and the precedent isn't encouraging.

**The Aqueducts**

Rome built its aqueducts during the centuries of expansion. Water crossed valleys and passed through mountains in precisely graded channels over a hundred kilometres, arriving by gravity alone, sustaining a city of over a million people. It's still impressive now, which is a strange thing to say about civil engineering from two thousand years ago.

By the fifth century Rome couldn't maintain them. No catastrophe had erased the knowledge, and nobody had forgotten how water flows downhill. What had degraded was the institutional capacity to organise complex projects. The administrative apparatus that coordinated labour, allocated resources, maintained standards and sustained political will across decades had slowly become less capable, and then incapable.

This is the thing I keep coming back to. The aqueducts crumbled because nobody could organise enough people, with enough resources, over enough time, to keep them running. The knowledge was institutional rather than individual. It lived in the way an organisation held a standard steady across a generation, which means it can be strong while every person involved is ordinary and can vanish while every person involved is brilliant. When the systems degraded the knowledge became unreachable, and nobody in Rome could have told you the year it happened.

**Institutional Sediment**

Early in a civilisation's life, building is relatively simple. Nothing about an aqueduct or a railway is ever easy, and simple here means only that the path from decision to completion runs fairly straight. Someone decides a thing should exist. Resources are allocated. Labour is organised. The thing gets built.

As the civilisation matures, layers of process accumulate. Safety regulations, which are individually reasonable. Environmental assessments, which are individually necessary. Community consultations, which are individually democratic. Legal frameworks for dispute resolution, which are individually just. Each layer arrives for good reasons, usually in response to a real failure. A building collapses, so codes are strengthened. A community is harmed, so consultation is required. Workers are exploited, so protections are mandated. I wouldn't remove most of them and neither would you.

But the layers interact in ways nobody designed and nobody fully understands. Each is thin. Each is individually invisible. Over decades the channel silts up, and the people working inside the institution don't notice, because every year looks much like the one before it. It's only when you hold today against thirty years ago that the scale of the accumulation appears.

By then reform is extraordinarily difficult, because every layer of sediment has acquired a constituency. The environmental assessment process employs environmental consultants. The consultation process employs engagement specialists. The compliance framework employs compliance officers. Removing a layer threatens their incomes and their professional identity, and they'll resist. There are no villains in this. They're people protecting what they have, and I'd resist too.

That asymmetry is the whole mechanism. Adding process is easy: it answers a visible failure and creates a constituency that will defend it forever. Removing process is hard: it requires overcoming a constituency and risks an invisible failure that someone will be blamed for. Nothing in the system corrects this, because there is no natural mechanism anywhere for the removal of a rule.

I've sat in meetings in Adelaide where a project that should take months was mapped onto years. The engineering was straightforward and the funding was there. What consumed the timeline was approvals: environmental assessment, heritage review, traffic study, community consultation, acoustic assessment and visual impact assessment, each taking months, each capable of generating objections requiring further assessment. Nobody in the room was incompetent. Everyone was doing exactly what the regulations required. The merits of the project were never in dispute.

**An Expiry Date**

The change I'd argue for is unglamorous and I think it would do more than anything else on offer: every process gets an expiry date.

Rules are written in response to conditions, and conditions change. A requirement that must be renewed on evidence every ten years is a requirement that can disappear without anyone having to be blamed for removing it. That last clause is the entire point. We currently have no way to delete a rule that doesn't require someone to stand up, argue against a constituency, and personally own the risk of an invisible failure. Sunset clauses make deletion the default and continuation the thing that needs an argument, which reverses the asymmetry that produced the sediment in the first place.

Alongside it, every approval should run on a clock. An assessment that must be answered in ninety days is an assessment. An assessment with no deadline is a veto held by whoever is slowest. And a deadline forces the standard to be written down in advance, which is exactly what an applicant needs in order to meet it.

We should also start counting delay as a cost. A business case counts what a project costs to build and says nothing about what it costs to wait, though both are real and both are paid by the public. Once the cost of delay appears on the page, somebody has to decide to pay it, which is a very different situation from nobody noticing it's being paid.

None of this is theoretical. Japan delivers infrastructure of extraordinary complexity on time and on budget with a regularity that seems fictional from Adelaide. The Shinkansen was built in the 1960s at a speed that would be literally impossible under current Australian frameworks. Japan isn't a lawless country - it has standards, protections and environmental law. What it also has are institutions that coordinate, decide and execute, so that process serves the project rather than consuming it. The advantage is institutional rather than cultural, which is the good news, because institutions can be copied and cultures cannot.

**Not a Law of Physics**

I don't know how this resolves. Technology might cut through the sediment - automation and digital government could lower the cost of compliance and shorten the path from decision to completion. Or technology might lay down sediment of its own, since digital systems create digital compliance and automated processes require automated oversight. I suspect which one we get depends on who holds the tools rather than on the tools themselves.

What I observe from Adelaide is a country visibly losing the ability to build. Not for lack of resources, or engineers, or even political will. Because the accumulated weight of our processes has made building so expensive, so slow and so uncertain that rational people increasingly decline to try, and a project never attempted never appears in any statistic.

The Romans didn't wake one morning unable to maintain their aqueducts. The capacity degraded gradually, over generations, slowly enough that each generation could tell itself things were roughly as they'd always been. By the time it was undeniable, the capacity to reverse it had gone as well.

I look at the Sydney light rail and I think we're early enough in the same pattern that it's still ours to break. What a society can build tells you which stage of it you're standing in - that's worth knowing, and it's uncomfortable to know. But none of this is a law of physics. The sediment accumulated because nobody ever built a mechanism to remove it, and mechanisms are the one thing a society is always free to build.
